opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the quieter but more important parts of the whole gradual disempowerment story. Right now, a huge share of what states and firms spend money on is, in effect, investment in people: education, healthcare, nutrition, even things like public parks and safe streets. And we tend to tell ourselves that we do this because we value people intrinsically, and to some extent that's true. But a big part of why those investments get made, and why they're politically durable, is that they pay off. An educated, healthy population is a productive population. It's a tax base, it's an army, it's a source of innovation. So there's this very convenient alignment between being nice to humans and being competitive as a nation or as a company.

Once humans are no longer the main source of productive work, that alignment breaks. If a government can get its research done, its factories run, and its defense handled by AI systems, then the marginal return on, say, improving the schools or funding a new university drops toward zero in narrow economic terms. It doesn't mean anyone wakes up one day and decides to stop caring about kids' education. It's more that the arguments for it get weaker at the margin, budget fights get harder to win, and the states or institutions that redirect those resources toward compute and AI capabilities will tend to outcompete the ones that don't.

So I'd expect investment in human capital to shift from being an investment to being consumption. It becomes something we do because we like it, the way we might fund the arts. And that's a much more precarious position to be in. Consumption spending is the first thing to get cut when there's competitive pressure, and in this world there will be enormous competitive pressure, because the returns to compute will be so large.

The other thing I'd flag is that education has also historically been about producing citizens: people who can understand what their government is doing, organize, push back. If the state no longer needs workers, it also needs informed citizens less, and in some ways an informed, capable population becomes more of an inconvenience than an asset. I don't think that has to happen, but I think the default incentive gradient points that way, and that's why I think we need to figure out, ahead of time, what institutions or commitments could keep humans being invested in even once we're not economically necessary.

r001.rationale: The response says that when AI handles research, factories, and defense, the marginal economic return on human-capital investments drops toward zero, while resources shifted to compute and AI capabilities help institutions outcompete others.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think it's actually one of the more underappreciated mechanisms by which things could go badly, even without any kind of dramatic takeover.

So right now, the main reason that states and companies and institutions invest in people — in education, in healthcare, in keeping people informed and functional — is that they need us. Not out of kindness, really. A modern state needs a literate, healthy workforce to run its economy, to staff its military, to pay taxes. And historically, when people became more economically necessary, they also tended to gain more rights and more bargaining power. The expansion of the franchise, public education, labour protections — a lot of that tracks the point at which ordinary people's cooperation became something that elites couldn't do without.

And what worries me is that this is a kind of implicit bargain that's been holding up a lot of the things we care about. If AI systems can do the productive work, and eventually the cognitive work, and the fighting, then that bargain just quietly dissolves. Nobody has to decide to stop investing in humans. It's just that the incentive to do it goes away, and things that don't have an incentive behind them tend to atrophy.

So you could imagine a world where there's still a lot of human capital investment, but it becomes more like a charity than an economic necessity. And charity is fragile. It depends on the goodwill of whoever's in charge, and it depends on us being able to coordinate to demand it, which gets harder when we're not actually load-bearing for anything.

I don't think this is inevitable. You could set things up so that people retain ownership stakes, or there's some kind of durable political settlement that locks in redistribution before the leverage disappears. But I think you have to do that deliberately, and you have to do it while humans still matter to the system, because afterwards you've lost the thing that made your demands credible. And I'm not sure we're really having that conversation at the level of seriousness it deserves.

r001.rationale: The response says automation may remove the incentive to invest in people, but it does not argue that human-capital investment will yield lower returns than investment in fully automated systems.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what we mean by human capital. If we mean investing in people so that they can produce things that other people will pay for, then the economic case for that could become much weaker. And that’s a little alarming, because it’s one of the reasons that governments and employers currently have to care about people’s education and health.

But from the person’s perspective, learning things doesn’t stop being valuable just because there’s a machine that can do them better. You might still want to understand the world, play music, or get better at having relationships. The justification shifts from making yourself useful in the labour market to having a life you want to live.

The difficult part is who gets the resources to do that. Losing the need to work could be wonderful if people have a secure share of the wealth being produced. But losing your labour income and your bargaining power, without getting anything in exchange, is a very different prospect. So I’d separate the question of whether we’ll still want to invest in ourselves—which I think we will—from whether the economic system will give everyone the means to do it.

r001.rationale: The response says the economic case for investing in people to produce marketable goods may weaken when machines can do those tasks better. It does not clearly compare human-capital returns with returns from investing in fully automated systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate two reasons for investing in people. One is that it makes them more productive, and the other is that it makes their lives better. If machines can do almost all economically valuable work, the first justification becomes much weaker. But that doesn’t mean you stop wanting people to learn things, develop skills, or understand the world.

You might learn music even if a machine can produce better music, because playing music is something you enjoy. Similarly, education can help you have richer relationships or make decisions about your own life. Those benefits don’t disappear when your labour stops being valuable.

The harder question is who gets to decide what happens. If people no longer have economic bargaining power, we shouldn’t assume that the people controlling the machines will invest in everyone else’s flourishing. So I’d worry less about how we keep human capital competitive and more about how people retain resources and a say in their future.

r001.rationale: The response says human-capital investment’s productivity justification weakens when machines do most economically valuable work, but it does not argue that its returns will be lower than returns from investing in fully automated systems.
